conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up during the first months postpartum. Everything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, so please feel free to be honest—we’ll take it one question at a time and go at your pace.

Ready to start?  
First, thinking back over the past seven days: overall, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Oh, I’ve definitely still been laughing—my husband and I were just giggling at the baby’s funny faces yesterday. I mean, I’m not laughing quite as often as before she was born, just because I’m tired, but when something’s funny it still hits me.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that sounds right—like I said, I can still laugh when something’s funny. It just might take a tiny bit more effort because I’m worn out, but the giggles are still there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do still look forward to stuff—like my mom’s coming over tomorrow and I’m excited for that. Sometimes the little outings feel like more work with the baby gear, but I still want to do them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If she spits up right after I change her or I can’t get her to nap, I might think, “Maybe I missed her cue,” but I don’t sit there beating myself up. I just try the next thing and move on.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if her breathing sounds normal or if the diaper rash is getting worse, even when everything looks fine. It’s not constant—just little spikes that pass once I check on her or distract myself with a chore.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
I haven’t had that panicky, can’t-catch-my-breath feeling. A few times I’ve gotten a quick “what-if” thought—like when she’s sleeping longer than usual—but it’s more a brief worry than real fear.
Things have been getting on top of me
Only a little. Some days the feedings, laundry, and trying to shower feel like they’re piling up, but I make a quick list, tackle one thing at a time, and it evens out.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s actually been one of the better parts—when she finally goes down, I can drift off pretty easily. I’m tired, sure, but not lying there feeling unhappy or wired.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t call it sad—more just really tired on some days. When she’s fussy for a long stretch I can feel a bit down in the moment, but it lifts once she settles or I get a short break.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I really haven’t cried much at all. Maybe once last week when I was extra tired and she wouldn’t latch, but it was just a couple of tears and I was fine once she fed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind, not even a little.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 8: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – EPDS Responses (10-item)

Symptoms endorsed
- Mild, situational worry/anxiety (items 4, 5): brief “what-if” thoughts about infant health, resolves quickly.
- Mild “things getting on top of me” (item 6) related to fatigue and daily tasks; no sense of being unable to cope.
- Transient low/frustrated mood when infant fussy (item 8) and single episode of tearfulness when fatigued (item 9).

Symptoms denied
- Loss of pleasure or interest, ability to laugh (items 1, 2).
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (item 3).
- Mood-related insomnia (item 7).
- Persistent sadness, crying spells (items 8, 9).
- Self-harm ideation (item 10) — zero reported; no safety concern identified.

Pattern
Overall score indicates minimal depressive or anxiety symptoms. Emotional functioning generally preserved; distress appears limited to normative postpartum fatigue and situational worry rather than pervasive mood or anxiety disorder.

Risk factors
- Postpartum fatigue and adjustment stress (low-grade).
- No other psychosocial risk factors elicited in this brief screen.

Screening impression
No evidence suggesting probable major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder at present. Continue routine perinatal support and re-screen if clinical picture changes.
